text: Before a language model can answer a single question, it spends weeks doing one humble thing: reading text and guessing the next token. That stage is called pretraining, and one of the surprising discoveries of recent years is that how well it will go can be forecast before the run begins, rather like predicting where a thrown ball will land from the first part of its flight. How can anyone forecast the loss of a model that does not exist yet?

Pretraining is the next-token game from earlier lessons, played at enormous scale. The model sees a window of text, assigns a probability to every token in its vocabulary, and pays the cross-entropy loss, which measures its surprise at the token that actually came next. Nobody writes labels, because the text supplies its own answers, and that is why every sentence on the web can become a training example.

How low that loss can go depends on how many parameters the model has, how many tokens it reads, and how much computation is spent, and the third ties the first two together. Each token costs about two operations per parameter on the forward pass and about four on the backward pass, so the whole training run costs roughly six times the parameters times the tokens.

In twenty twenty, Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI trained models across a vast range of sizes and found that the test loss falls as a power law in each of these quantities, provided the other two are not holding it back. A power law is a rule where multiplying the input by some factor always multiplies the output by the same fixed factor, wherever you start, like the period of a pendulum as you lengthen its string. On a plot with logarithmic axes, such a rule becomes a straight line, and a straight line is something you can extend with a ruler.

The ruler comes with two honest warnings. The slope is shallow, so every further step down in loss costs a multiplied amount of compute, which is why frontier training runs are so expensive. And the line cannot fall forever, because text is partly unpredictable even to a perfect reader. Later fits therefore add a constant floor, the irreducible loss, and describe the rest as two shrinking terms, one for the size of the model and one for the amount of data.

So, with a fixed budget, should you build a bigger model or feed it more text? Kaplan's fits advised growing the model much faster than the data. In twenty twenty-two, Hoffmann and colleagues at DeepMind repeated the study, this time matching each run's learning rate schedule to its length, and concluded that parameters and tokens should grow in equal proportion. Their model, Chinchilla, was a quarter of the size of their earlier model Gopher and read more than four times as much text for the same compute, and it outperformed Gopher on a large range of tasks.

Compute optimal is not the whole story, though, because a model is trained once and then queried an enormous number of times. The first Llama paper from Meta deliberately trained smaller models on far more tokens than that balance suggests, paying more during training to get a model that is cheaper to serve, and reported that its smallest model was still improving after a trillion tokens.

Keep in mind that these laws forecast the loss, not any particular skill, and performance on an individual task can move far less smoothly than the curve beneath it. A predictable loss is still what lets a lab plan a run before paying for it. What comes out is a superb completer of text, but not yet an assistant, and turning one into the other is the subject of the next lesson, fine-tuning and instruction tuning.
